sections.title: The Stringency of the Prohibition of Gentile Wine
sections.html:
Since wine is the most important and most gladdening drink, and its power to release a person from inhibitions, to draw hearts close and to arouse joy is great, the Torah commanded that it be poured as a libation together with the sacrifices, so that we may draw close to God with this special power as well. Likewise the Sages instituted that a blessing be recited over a cup of wine at every joyous occasion of a mitzva: at Kiddush and Havdala of Shabbat and festivals, at betrothal and marriage, at a brit mila and a pidyon ha-ben, so that the joy of the holiness of all these mitzvot would be revealed in the body and its sensations as well. On the other hand, since the influence of wine is great, the danger in its improper use is very great, and people of lust became addicted to drinking it and committed all the abominations while drunk. And idolaters poured it as a libation to their idols in the hope that they would help them fulfill all their desires. Therefore, the Sages were exceedingly stringent regarding wine, and when they decreed a prohibition on the wine, bread and cooked dishes of gentiles, they were stringent to regard wine that gentiles prepared, which is called "stam yeinam" (their ordinary wine), like wine that they poured as a libation to their idols, which is forbidden even for benefit. Not only that, but they decreed that even a Jew's wine that an idolatrous gentile touched in the manner in which they used to touch wine when pouring a libation to their idols would be forbidden for benefit.

It turns out, then, that there are two stringencies in the prohibition of wine compared with the prohibition of the bread and cooking of gentiles. The first: since wine may create excessive closeness, in order to distance Israel from assimilation they forbade even a Jew's wine that a gentile touched, even though he did not intend by his touch to pour it as a libation to idolatry. The second: wine that an idolatrous gentile touched was forbidden even for benefit and not only for drinking, like the law of wine poured as a libation to idolatry, which is forbidden for benefit by Torah law, for this is the way of the Sages, to make the prohibitions uniform, so that Israel would be able to remember the halakha and keep it without confusing the laws.

Wine that is forbidden for benefit may not be sold to a gentile or even given to him as a gift, for there is benefit even from giving a gift.1

sections.title: A Gentile Who Does Not Engage in Idolatry
sections.html:
When the gentile does not engage in idolatry, there is no concern that he poured the wine as a libation to idolatry, but the concern of assimilation exists, and therefore the Sages forbade his wine for drinking but not for benefit. That is, on the one hand, because of the special stringency regarding wine, which has the power to blur the boundaries needed for preserving Jewish distinctiveness, they were stringent to forbid wine through his touch. And on the other hand, since he does not engage in idolatry, they forbade his wine, and the wine he touched, for drinking but not for benefit. Thus the first stringency of the prohibition of wine applies to him, and therefore his touch too forbids the wine, whereas the second stringency, according to which the wine is forbidden for benefit as well, does not apply to him (SA 124:1, 6).

This is the rule: the law of a gentile who does not engage in idolatry is one degree more lenient than that of a gentile who engages in idolatry. Therefore, whatever is forbidden for benefit with an idolater is forbidden for drinking with a gentile who does not engage in idolatry, and whatever is forbidden only for drinking with an idolater is permitted with a gentile who does not engage in idolatry (SA 124:7).2

As we shall learn in the next halakha, today the law of a gentile who does not engage in idolatry is more common; however, in the course of our study we shall deal mainly with the law of idolaters, with whom the Sages dealt in the Mishna and Talmud, and from this the law of a gentile who does not engage in idolatry, whose law is one degree more lenient, will be clarified.

sections.title: Muslims, Christians and Hindus
sections.html:
A Muslim, even though he denies the Torah, since he believes in one God without idolatrous partnership (shittuf), is not considered an idolater, and therefore the wine he prepared or the wine he touched is forbidden for drinking and permitted for benefit (as explained in note 2). And likewise is the law of a secular gentile, and likewise the law of members of the Druze religion.

Regarding Christians, the poskim disagreed. According to the stringent opinion, since they believe that "that man" too is God, they associate idolatry in their faith, and therefore wine they touched becomes forbidden for benefit (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Asurot 11:7). And some are lenient and hold that since in practice they are not accustomed to pour wine as a libation to idolatry, wine that they touch is forbidden only for drinking and not for benefit (Rashi, Rashbam). And some of the Rishonim are lenient in this because in their opinion the Christians of their time were already not considered complete idolaters, since their religion is more abstract than that of ordinary idolaters (Meiri). In practice, ab initio the custom follows the stringent opinion, and in a time of pressing need one relies on the lenient opinion. And it seems that even according to the stringent opinion, Christians who believe that "that man" was a messenger and not God are not considered idolaters, and according to all opinions the wine they touch is permitted for benefit.

Hindus and members of other religions whose worshippers bow down to statues and offer them offerings are considered idolaters. However, according to the approach of the lenient opinion, since they are not accustomed to pour wine as a libation to their idols, their touch of wine forbids it for drinking but not for benefit. In a time of pressing need, one may rely on their opinion.3

sections.title: What Is Wine
sections.html:
As long as the liquid coming out of the grapes is still mixed with the seeds and skins, it does not have the law of wine, and if a gentile touched it – it does not become forbidden. Once the liquid has begun to separate from them, that is, it has flowed to the side where it remains without seeds and skins, it has the law of wine. And then all the other liquids in the winepress also have the law of wine, and if a gentile touched the liquids, or the wet seeds or skins in the winepress, he has forbidden everything in the winepress. Not only that, but even if one cup of wine, strained of seeds and skins, was taken from the winepress, from that moment the law of wine applies to everything that remains in the winepress (SA 123:17-18).

Wine that has turned into vinegar does not become forbidden through a gentile's touch. When there is a doubt whether the wine has already become complete vinegar, it is tested by pouring it on the ground: if it bubbles and ferments due to its contact with the limestone material – this is a sign that it has become vinegar (SA 123:6).

The wine that becomes forbidden through libation or a gentile's touch is wine in its natural form, but if it has changed from its nature, it does not become forbidden, for the gentiles were not accustomed to pour it as a libation. Therefore, wine diluted with water, as long as the wine is more than a sixth of the water, has the law of wine, and a gentile's touch forbids it, since it is the nature of wine that it is customarily diluted. But if its proportion is lower than this, the law of wine no longer applies to it (SA 134:5).

Similarly, wine into which sugar or honey was mixed to sweeten it, or pepper to make it sharp, if its taste has changed from its natural taste, does not become forbidden through a gentile's touch, since the gentiles did not pour it as a libation to their idols. But wine into which a little sugar or honey or another flavor was mixed, and its taste changed only slightly, if a gentile touches it – it becomes forbidden (SA 123:4).

In general, the wines whose natural taste is preserved are dry wines, semi-dry wines, and wines that are slightly sweet. And although a little sugar is mixed into them or a little alcohol is added to them, their natural taste is preserved. But in very sweet wines, such as the simple sweet wines, much sugar is mixed in and their taste has changed, and therefore a gentile's touch does not forbid them.4

sections.title: Cooked Wine
sections.html:
Wine that has been cooked does not become forbidden through a gentile's touch, since idolaters did not pour cooked wine as a libation to their idols, and wine that is not fit for libation does not become forbidden through a gentile's touch. However, if the gentile touched the wine before it was cooked, since it had already become forbidden, the cooking will not save it from its prohibition (Avoda Zara 29b).

The poskim disagreed as to when wine is considered cooked, and many definitions have been given for this. In practice there are two opinions. According to the stringent opinion, from the moment its taste changes noticeably, as happens after the wine boils and remains on the fire until its liquids are noticeably reduced due to evaporation. And according to the lenient opinion, from the moment it reaches a heat that begins to change its taste, and this happens after the wine reaches a heat of about seventy degrees, when the alcohol in the wine begins to evaporate. And since the prohibition of gentile wine is rabbinic, the halakha follows the lenient opinion.

However, the poskim of our time disagreed regarding pasteurized wine and grape juice, that is, where the grape juice or wine was heated to a temperature of about seventy to eighty degrees in order to disinfect it of bacteria and yeasts, so that it can no longer ferment and will remain in its taste without change. Some are stringent because the taste does not change through this. And although the alcohol begins to evaporate, since the pasteurization is performed in closed vessels, the alcohol returns to the wine, and consequently its taste does not change. Moreover, one should take into account the stringent opinion, which holds that only if much of the liquid of the wine has evaporated and its taste has changed noticeably is it not subject to the prohibition (Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach, Or Le-Tziyon, Rav Yosef Shalom Elyashiv). On the other hand, some hold that since in practice the wine reached a level of heat that cooks it, and the alcohol in it began to evaporate, it has changed from its nature and is not subject to the prohibition. And although afterwards the alcohol that evaporated returned to the wine, since there was a stage at which it left the wine, its law is that of cooked wine. In addition, connoisseurs feel that its taste is slightly impaired (Igrot Moshe, Rav Goren, Yabi'a Omer, Minḥat Yitzḥak). And since the basis of the prohibition is rabbinic, the halakha follows the lenient opinion. Those who wish to be meticulous are stringent. However, in a situation where an insult might be caused to someone whom it is not proper to insult, even one who wishes to be meticulous should act according to the lenient opinion.5

sections.title: Touching Wine
sections.html:
As we learned (halakha 1), the Sages decreed that any touch by an idolatrous gentile of a Jew's wine, similar to the manner in which the gentiles were accustomed to pour libations to idols, forbids the wine for benefit. Their manner of libation was to agitate the wine, that is, to move it with a hand or a stick. Likewise they were accustomed to pour libations by touching with the mouth while drinking, for while drinking they intended to move the wine slightly and thereby pour it as a libation to the idols. And even when it is clear that the gentile did not intend by his touching or his drinking to pour the wine as a libation to idols, since he is an idolater and touched the wine in the way idolaters used to pour libations to idols, the wine is forbidden for benefit. And if the touching was done by a gentile who does not engage in idolatry, the wine is forbidden for drinking but not for benefit (SA 124:11).6

If he touched the wine without intention, for example his hand was inadvertently dipped into the wine, or he thought it was beer and intended to touch the beer – the wine is forbidden for drinking but not for benefit (SA 124:10). If the unintentional touching was by a gentile who does not engage in idolatry – the wine is permitted for drinking (SA 124:7).

When there is a doubt whether the gentile touched the wine intentionally, one is lenient, since it is a rabbinic doubt (Shakh 124:33). And likewise in any doubt concerning the law of yayin nesekh, one is lenient.7

sections.title: Agitating Wine by Shaking the Vessel
sections.html:
Some say that idolaters had an additional manner of libation, by agitating wine in an open vessel, that is, shaking the vessel forcefully in order to move the wine inside it. And the Sages decreed that if an idolatrous gentile agitated it in this manner, even not for the sake of libation, the wine is forbidden for benefit. And if he does not engage in idolatry, the wine is forbidden for drinking. But if the vessel containing the wine was closed, even with a temporary stopper or a plastic bag, the wine does not become forbidden at all, for there is no manner of libation with a closed vessel (Rambam, Rivam, Ramban, Rosh, SA and Rema 124:17). And if an idolatrous gentile lifted the open vessel and walked with it, and even went up stairs, and the wine in the vessel moved forcefully, since it moved due to walking – the wine is permitted. Likewise, if the wine moved as a result of pulling out the bottle's cork – the wine is permitted. Thus, in their opinion, only shaking the vessel and agitating the wine inside it without reason forbids the wine.

On the other hand, some are lenient and hold that it was not customary to pour libations with a vessel, and therefore moving wine inside a vessel does not forbid it (Ra'avad, Rashba, Rabbeinu Yeruḥam, Meiri, Rivash, Maharashdam, Baḥ, Taz and Knesset Ha-gedola).

In practice, regarding an idolatrous gentile, ab initio the custom follows the stringent opinion, and in a case of loss one is lenient regarding benefit. And with a gentile who does not engage in idolatry, one is not stringent about agitating in a vessel at all.8

sections.title: Koḥo (His Force) – Pouring Wine
sections.html:
If an idolatrous gentile poured wine from a bottle into a cup, all the wine in the cup and in the bottle is forbidden for drinking and permitted for benefit. It is not forbidden for benefit, since he did not touch it with his hand, nor did he agitate it in the vessel. And it is forbidden for drinking because the Sages forbade wine that the gentile poured by his force (koḥo). And since the stream came out of the bottle continuously into the cup, a "nitzok" (poured stream) connection was created between the wine in the cup and the wine that remained in the bottle, and the wine in the bottle too is forbidden for drinking. However, in a situation of great loss, for example where he poured the wine from a large vessel, the wine that remained in the large vessel is kosher for drinking (SA and Rema 125:1; 126:1-2).9

And if a gentile who does not engage in idolatry poured from the bottle into the cup, according to many, the wine in the cup and in the bottle is permitted for drinking (Shakh 124:11; Dagul Me-revava, Rabbi Akiva Eiger, Erekh Ha-shulḥan, Ish Matzli'aḥ, Ḥazon Ish). And some are stringent and forbid the wine in the cup for drinking and permit the wine that remained in the bottle (Taz; Yabi'a Omer YD 1:11). And although according to the rules of halakha one should rule according to the lenient opinion, many are accustomed to be stringent. And some are even accustomed to be stringent regarding what remained in the bottle.

In practice, the main ruling follows the lenient opinion, but one should not employ gentiles to pour wine, since it is difficult to supervise that they do not touch the wine. Therefore the custom is that when the waiter is a gentile, even though he does not engage in idolatry, the diners open the bottle and pour for themselves. However, after the fact, if the waiter opened the bottle and poured for them, the wine is kosher, and all the more so the wine that remained in the bottle is kosher. For as long as they did not see him agitating the wine in the bottle or touching the wine in it, it is permitted to drink the wine (as explained above in halakha 6 and note 7; and the details of the halakha here are below, at the end of the note).10

sections.title: Guarding the Wine
sections.html:
When a Jew wishes to deposit his wine with an idolatrous gentile, he must place the wine closed in a vessel with two seals. As long as the vessel remains closed with the two seals – the wine in it is kosher, and if the seals were opened – the wine is forbidden. When the gentile does not engage in idolatry, one seal is sufficient. A seal means a special closure that is difficult to forge. For example, one can stick adhesive tape over the opening of the bottle and sign across the place of attachment, so that if the tape is opened, it will be difficult to restore the signature to its original form. And if he sticks another piece of tape over the opening and signs on it too, it will be considered two seals. A seal can also be a special knot of a plastic bag, which it is difficult for one who opens the bottle to restore to its exact form. In order to seal the bottle with two seals, factories are accustomed to seal wine bottles with a cork or metal stopper, and over this they stick another plastic wrapping.

If an idolatrous gentile stayed alone with a bottle of wine that is not sealed with two seals, the wine is forbidden for benefit, even if he stayed with it for a short time, for since the gentiles were accustomed to pour wine as libations, the Sages decreed that any wine that a gentile could have poured as a libation would be forbidden as though he had poured it. But if the gentile does not engage in idolatry, there is no concern that he will want to pour it as a libation. However, if he stayed alone with the wine, and there is a concern that he will drink from the wine directly from the mouth of the bottle or touch the wine inside it – the wine is forbidden for drinking, and only if it was sealed with one seal is it not forbidden. And if there is no concern that he will drink from the wine or touch it – the wine is kosher even without a seal (SA 128:1; Rema 4; Shakh 1). According to many, the law of an idolatrous gentile who is not accustomed to pour wine as a libation is like the law of a gentile who does not engage in idolatry.11

If they warned the gentile not to touch the wine bottles at all, and if he violates their warning he will be considered a thief who may be punished for it, for example his terms of employment may be harmed – even if they left him alone in the house and the bottle of wine is not sealed, as long as there is a possibility that they will suddenly come in and see him touching the wine, or see him through a window or by means of a closed-circuit camera, the wine is permitted. But if there was a time when the gentile knew that there was no chance that they would see him, since he could then have drunk from the wine without being caught as a thief – the wine is forbidden (SA 128:4; 129:1). Therefore, one who employs a gentile in his home, and there are times when the gentile is alone in the house and might drink from the wine, must take care that the wine bottles are sealed properly, or lock them in a cupboard that the gentile has no possibility of managing to open. And if he did not do so, the wine is forbidden. And if the wine is cooked or sweetened, it does not have the law of yayin nesekh, and it need not be guarded.12

sections.title: Additional Laws
sections.html:
In order to distance Israel from the prohibition, the Sages instructed that ab initio, when gentiles harvest grapes for a Jew, care should be taken to place the grapes in vessels that have holes, so that liquids that come out of the grapes will not collect at the bottom of the vessel. But after the fact, if they harvested into vessels and liquids collected at the bottom of the vessel and the gentile touched them, they are not forbidden, since they had not yet been separated from the grapes. Similarly, ab initio one should not let a gentile carry grapes to the winepress, and one should not let him pour the grapes into the winepress, lest he touch the wine in the winepress; and after the fact, if he threw them into the winepress, he did not forbid the winepress (Avoda Zara 59b; SA 125:6). And some wrote that even with a mechanical harvester, ab initio a Jew should operate it, since during the harvest liquids squeezed from the grapes collect in the harvester's container. However, after the fact, even in their opinion there is no prohibition in this, since these liquids have not been separated from the seeds and skins (Rav Eliyahu; Bein Yisrael La-amim 21:3).

Everything the Sages decreed regarding wine that a gentile touched applies when the gentile did not intend to provoke the Jew and cause him to lose his wine; but if he touched the wine in order to harm the Jew and forbid his wine, the Sages did not decree, and the wine is permitted for drinking. On the contrary, the Jew should make an effort to drink the wine in front of the gentile, so that he will know that he did not succeed by his actions in disqualifying the wine (Tosafot Avoda Zara 58b, s.v. "Katav"; Beit Yosef 132:1; Rema 124:27).

sections.title: Alcoholic Beverages
sections.html:
After the Sages forbade the wine, bread and cooking of gentiles, the Amoraim added a further safeguard against assimilation, that a Jew should not drink an alcoholic beverage in a gentile's home, or in his shop, or in his café, or in any place in his domain (Avoda Zara 31b). Included in the prohibition are all alcoholic beverages, such as whiskey, arak, vodka, liqueur, beer and the like. The prohibition applies even when the Jew drinks the beverage alone, without company with the gentile, since the drink loosens a person and may bring down the dignified barrier that should fence in Israel. There was no need to decree this in the days of the Tanna'im in the Land of Israel, because their drinking was mainly wine, and regarding it they established severe decrees; but in Babylonia, where people were accustomed to drink alcoholic beverages of other kinds, they needed to forbid these beverages as well (Arukh Ha-shulḥan 114:6).

There is a difference between the decree on the bread and cooked dishes of gentiles and the prohibition of drinking alcoholic beverages at a gentile's: the prohibition of eating the bread and cooked dishes of gentiles applies to the bread and cooked dish prepared by gentiles, and it is forbidden to eat them even in a Jewish home. But regarding a beverage, the prohibition is not on the beverage but on drinking it at the gentile's. Therefore, even if a Jew prepared a beverage and brought it himself to the gentile's home, he is forbidden to drink it in the gentile's home, even if he drinks it alone. On the other hand, not in the gentile's home, a Jew is permitted to drink a beverage that a gentile prepared from kosher ingredients (SA 114:1). And it is not subject to the prohibition of bishulei goyim, since it consists mainly of water (above 28:7). That is, the aim of the prohibition of drinking alcoholic beverages at a gentile's is to prevent the closeness that may develop while drinking.13

However, on a temporary basis for a great need it is permitted. For example, when a Jew needs to drink a little alcoholic beverage in order to strengthen himself or to prevent headaches, he is permitted to enter a gentile's bar, buy one glass, drink it and leave. Likewise, if he happened to be in a gentile's home for another purpose and they offered him a drink, and he especially needs it, he is permitted to drink one glass, on condition that they do not sit together to drink (SA 114:1). And if he has already been compelled to drink twice in a gentile's bar or home, even if he will need it, he should not drink with them a third time, for he has already gone from temporary drinking to regular drinking, and there is concern that this will lead to excessive closeness (Knesset Ha-gedola; Pri Ḥadash 4; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 6).

One who has to travel from his home to another place and is lodging in a gentile's home, whether for payment or for free, may bring a drink with him and drink it in the gentile's home, for at that time the gentile's home is considered his home. But he should not buy a drink from the host and drink it there. And if the host offers him a little drink, so that enmity will not arise between them, he is permitted to accept and drink a little (Tosafot Avoda Zara 31b, s.v. "Ve-tarvayhu"; SA 114:1; Shakh 2). Only with a beverage were they lenient to drink on a temporary basis in order to prevent enmity, but there is no permission to eat the bread and cooked dishes of gentiles in order to prevent enmity (Taz 152:1).

Regarding drinking coffee and tea, the poskim disagreed. Some say that since these too are customarily drunk in company and drinking them draws hearts close, it is forbidden to drink them in a gentile's home (Radbaz, the Arizal, Ḥokhmat Adam 66:14). And some say that there is no prohibition to drink them in a gentile's home, since the prohibition applies only to an alcoholic beverage. This is on condition that their sitting there does not involve frivolity (Pri Ḥadash 114:6; Ḥatam Sofer, Avoda Zara 31b; Ben Ish Ḥai, Year Two, Ḥukat 16). In practice, as a matter of friendship – it is proper to be stringent; and as a matter of respect for the host – one may be lenient.

sections.title: A Party of Gentiles
sections.html:
At a gathering of gentiles for raising a toast, a Jew is forbidden to drink even a little alcoholic beverage, even if the drinking takes place in a public hall that does not belong to the gentile, and even if the Jew brought the beverage from his home. But there is no prohibition to eat from the light refreshments served there, on condition that they are kosher. And if it is a gathering of Jews, even if there were gentiles at it, since most of the participants are Jews – it is permitted even to drink an alcoholic beverage (based on Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Asurot 17:10).

At a party of gentiles, since the meal is more important, not only a beverage is forbidden, but even kosher food may not be eaten there. Even if the gentile host set aside a table for the Jews on which mehadrin kosher food is served, it is forbidden to eat there. Included in a party are: a wedding, a party in honor of a birth, and all the more so a meal in honor of a holiday, such as Christmas, New Year's Eve (Sylvester) and Eid al-Adha (the Festival of the Sacrifice). But for an ordinary meal without special festivity, it is permitted to be a guest in a gentile's home or to dine with him in a restaurant, on condition that the food is kosher and the Jew is careful not to drink alcohol (Levush; Ḥokhmat Adam 87:12).

The prohibition of dining at a party of gentiles too is intended to serve as a barrier against assimilation. And so we learned that the Torah warned against participating in the meals of gentiles because of the concern of assimilation, as it is stated (Shemot 34:15-16): "Lest you make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land … and one call you and you eat of his sacrifice (his meal); and you take of his daughters for your sons, and his daughters go astray after their gods and make your sons go astray after their gods." And when it is a party of an idolatrous gentile, participating in his meal also involves supporting his religion. And concerning this the Sages said (Avoda Zara 8a): "Jews outside the Land are idol worshippers in purity (that is, influenced by the culture of their religion). How so? A gentile who made a feast for his son and invited all the Jews in his city – even though they eat their own food and drink their own drink and their own attendant stands before them, Scripture regards them as though they ate of the sacrifices to the dead" (sacrifices of idolatry). And likewise the Sages said that the decree in the days of Haman was decreed on Israel because they enjoyed the feast of Aḥashverosh (see Megilla 12a; Yalkut Shimoni, Esther 1056).

However, the foods that were served at the party are not forbidden, and therefore if the gentile sent some of them to a Jew's home, and it is clear that they are kosher without question, the Jew is permitted to eat them (SA YD 152:1-2).

When there is a concern that refraining from participating in a wedding or a party will cause enmity, the poskim disagreed whether it is permitted to participate in the party and taste the kosher foods. Some say that it is forbidden, since the main concern is lest they come to intermarriage and assimilation, and consequently the concern of enmity does not cancel this; on the contrary, it is good that distance be created between them (Taz 152:1). And some say that it is permitted, and there is no need to be concerned about cultural influence, since the participation is only because of enmity (see Nekudot Ha-kesef there). In practice, the accepted custom is to try to avoid it as much as possible, and to give a nice gift and heartfelt good wishes instead of participating in the party. And when there is no possibility of avoiding it, one relies on the lenient opinions and participates to the small extent required to prevent enmity and maintain good relations. In any case, all alcoholic drinking is forbidden.14

sections.title: A Jew Who Desecrates Shabbat
sections.html:
The attitude toward desecration of Shabbat is especially severe, to the point that the Sages said that one may not accept a sacrifice from a Jew who publicly desecrates Shabbat, his slaughtering is invalid, and he invalidates the eruv like a gentile (Ḥullin 5a; Eruvin 69b). Based on this, the Rambam wrote (Hilkhot Shabbat 30:15): "Shabbat and idolatry – each of the two is equal to all the other mitzvot of the Torah. And Shabbat is the sign between the Holy One, blessed be He, and us forever. Therefore, whoever transgresses the other mitzvot is included among the wicked of Israel, but one who publicly desecrates Shabbat is like an idolater, and both are like gentiles in all respects." Similarly, several Rishonim wrote that wine that a Jew who publicly desecrates Shabbat touched is forbidden like wine that a gentile who does not engage in idolatry touched, which is forbidden for drinking and permitted for benefit (Behag, Rabbeinu Yona, Eshkol, Rivash and others).

And although many Rishonim did not mention this law, the Aḥaronim agreed in halakha that wine that one who publicly desecrates Shabbat touched is forbidden for drinking. And although the prohibition of wine that a gentile touched is because of the concern of assimilation, which is not relevant with regard to Jews who desecrate Shabbat, since for several laws they equated one who desecrates Shabbat with a gentile, they applied the stringency of this law to them as well. Moreover, they forbade their touch as a penalty and a protest against those who transgress such a severe transgression. For Shabbat was the most distinct expression of Jewish identity, and whoever dared to desecrate Shabbat publicly thereby committed a terrible act of defiance against the faith of Israel, and announced before the whole world that he does not identify with Judaism.

However, only if he touched the wine itself or drank from it does the wine become forbidden; but if he poured from the bottle into the cup, the wine does not become forbidden, for this is the law according to most poskim even with a gentile who does not engage in idolatry. Admittedly, some are stringent regarding a gentile, but regarding a Jew there is no room to be stringent (above, 8). All the more so if he moved the cup from place to place, the wine does not become forbidden, for even an idolatrous gentile does not forbid the wine in this manner (above, 7).

In recent generations the question of the attitude toward those who publicly desecrate Shabbat has arisen anew. For, to our great sorrow, many Jews began to desecrate Shabbat, until a situation arose in which Shabbat is no longer the expression that characterizes Jewish identity. Not only that, but whereas in the past the protest against Shabbat desecrators was effective in preventing them from breaching the fence, in recent generations the protest has generally distanced more than it has fenced in. Therefore many of the later poskim were lenient in a time of need, and ruled that only one who desecrates Shabbat demonstratively, in order to provoke and defy the tradition, is considered like a gentile, but one who honors Shabbat with Kiddush and lighting candles is not considered like a gentile. Moreover, if he is a Jew who did not merit a Torah education, he is like one acting under duress, since he does not understand the severity of desecrating Shabbat. And even if he grew up in a religious home, sometimes the secular influence is so strong that he is close to being considered one who acts unwittingly and under duress, who cannot withstand the spirit of the times, and he should not be regarded as a gentile (Binyan Tziyon Ḥadashot 23; Melamed Le-ho'il OḤ 29; Igrot Ha-Re'aya vol. 1, letter 138). Moreover, stringency in these distancings may cause insults and disputes in families and communities (Rav Yosef Mashash).

And although some are stringent even in our time, with the aim of preventing the influence of Shabbat desecrators on those who observe the mitzvot, it is agreed in practice by most poskim that in a time of need, in order to prevent insult or harm to the brotherhood that should exist among Israel, one should not be stringent regarding wine that Shabbat desecrators touched, as long as they do not do so to provoke. And likewise, if he wishes, he is counted in a minyan (Peninei Halakha: Tefilla 2:8).15

sections.title: The Prohibition of Drinking Frivolously
sections.html:
One should not drink an alcoholic beverage out of frivolity or in the company of frivolous people, because the influence of alcohol is great, and therefore the Sages instructed to be very careful with it. As we learned in the Torah, even a perfectly righteous man like Noaḥ, when he was not careful with wine, stumbled and fell into the depths of shame and disgrace. Likewise Lot, through drinking, came to illicit relations with his daughters (Bereishit Rabba 36:4). Likewise Nadav and Avihu, the sons of Aharon the Kohen, who were righteous like their father and were supposed to inherit his place, since they were not careful with wine and entered the Mishkan intoxicated, were punished and died (Vayikra Rabba 12:1). And the Sages said (Sanhedrin 70a): "There is nothing that brings wailing upon a person except wine." They further said that wine may bring a person to transgression and illicit relations, and therefore one who fears that his inclination will overpower him should make himself a nazir, abstaining from wine (Nazir 2a). When they said "wine," they meant alcohol, for in their time alcohol was drunk mainly as wine.

When alcohol is drunk in a group with music, the concern greatly increases that a person will become wild, forget his purpose and be drawn after his desires. Many evils, including the exile, came upon Israel as a result of this. As it is stated (Yeshayahu 5:11-15): "Woe to those who rise early in the morning to pursue strong drink, who tarry late into the night till wine inflames them. And the lyre and the harp, the timbrel and the flute, and wine are at their feasts; but they do not regard the work of the Lord, nor have they seen the work of His hands. Therefore My people have gone into exile for lack of knowledge, and their honored men are famished (its dignitaries will die of hunger), and their multitude is parched with thirst (in place of the wine they drank). Therefore Sheol has enlarged its appetite and opened its mouth without measure (without limit), and her splendor and her multitude and her tumult, and he who exults in her, go down into it. And man is bowed down, and man is humbled, and the eyes of the haughty are humbled" (Sota 48a).

However, wine also has a good side, in that it can give expression to true joy (above, 1). As it is stated in the chapter of thanksgiving to God, that among the good things God gave man He also gave wine, as it is stated (Tehillim 104:1-15): "Bless the Lord, O my soul … and wine that gladdens the heart of man." And the Sages said (Berakhot 35a): "Song is recited only over wine." Therefore they instituted reciting Kiddush over a cup of wine on Shabbatot and festivals, at weddings and britot. And as stated in the Zohar (vol. 3, 189b): "There is no sanctification except with wine, and there is no blessing except with wine."

Thus the distinction is between joy and drinking of a mitzva and joy and drinking of the mundane, as the Sages said (Shabbat 30b) that the proper joy is the joy of a mitzva, as it is stated (Kohelet 8:15): "So I commended joy, for a man has no better thing under the sun than to eat, and to drink, and to be joyful, and that this should accompany him in his labor all the days of his life which God has given him under the sun." But one must beware of joy that is not of a mitzva, as it is stated (ibid. 2:2): "I said of laughter, 'It is mad,' and of joy, 'What does it accomplish?'", for this laughter is "mehulal," that is, mixed with weeping and sighing, and this joy ends in sorrow (Rashi there). And when mundane drinking is done in a group, it is more disgraceful and is considered "a seat of scorners," as it is stated (Mishlei 20:1): "Wine is a mocker, strong drink is riotous, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise." Rabbeinu Yona explained (Sha'arei Teshuva 3:177): "Drinking wine causes three bad things: a) that the man becomes a scoffer; b) that he becomes riotous and a man of many words, and our Sages of blessed memory said (Avot 1:17): 'And whoever multiplies words brings sin…'; c) 'and whoever is led astray by it is not wise.'"

And likewise the Sages ruled in halakha that it is forbidden to sing or play musical instruments while drinking wine, and only for songs and praises to God, or when engaged in a mitzva meal such as a wedding, is it permitted to sing and play (SA OḤ 560:3).16

Therefore, one should not drink in clubs and at parties of friends in a secular atmosphere, for one who is drawn after such drinking may become distanced from Torah and mitzvot and come to transgression. And this is what the Sages meant: "Keep far from a bad neighbor, and do not associate with the wicked" (Avot 1:7). Admittedly, it is possible that those who drink frivolously in pubs and clubs conduct themselves like righteous people in other areas, and then it is proper to create cooperation and friendships with them. But in a place where they are accustomed to drink frivolously, the bad aspects of casting off Torah and mitzvot come to expression, and at that time they are considered bad company who may draw one away from the ways of Torah and mitzvot. And concerning this it is stated (Tehillim 1:1): "Happy is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of scorners." The Sages explained (Avoda Zara 18b) that a person should not say, "I will go only once to a feast of scorners," for if he goes – he will end up standing there, and if he stands – he will end up sitting there and becoming a scorner.

Sometimes a person is invited by his workplace to a secular event conducted in an atmosphere of frivolity, and when possible, it is preferable to refrain from participating in such an event. And if there is no possibility of refraining from it, at the very least one should take care not to drink alcoholic beverages there.
